rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Rainwater harvesting catches rain on roofs and small slopes, filters it, and stores it in tanks or sends it underground through pits, wells and check dams. The water table rises and dry months are easier. Wasteland in this topic is degraded land — eroded, saline, waterlogged or mined — and it is repaired by matching the fix to the damage: cover, contour bunds, drainage and a pause in grazing.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Roof → first-flush or filter → tank, or → recharge pit / well.
Degraded slope → trees and grasses + contour bunds + rest from grazing → cover that holds soil.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Harvesting rain is not the same as building a large dam on a river. The catchment here is a roof or a small slope.  ·  Wasteland is not unused land that was always poor. In this topic it means degraded land.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Tamil Nadu's compulsory rooftop rule is the standard textbook example of a law. Nepal's ponds are the local example.  ·  Do not call every barren rock a wasteland created by people. Stick to eroded, saline, mined or waterlogged land.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: A school roof piped into a covered tank supplies washing water through the dry months.  ·  A check dam on a small stream holds monsoon water long enough for it to soak toward the wells below.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: A recharge pit is not a rubbish pit. It is for clean rainwater. Waste in the pit pollutes the groundwater.  ·  Planting trees on a wasteland fails if the goats immediately eat the seedlings. Protection is part of the method.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Sketch the path from a roof to a tank and mark the filter.  ·  Match erosion, salinity and mining spoil with one repair each.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Harvest = catch and store or recharge. Wasteland = degraded land, restored with cover and water control.  ·  Filter first. Then store.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: How does a check dam raise a water table?  ·  Why is overgrazing a cause of wasteland and also a reason restoration fails?

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Treat the question as two halves if it names both practices. Do not answer only the water half.  ·  Name one traditional structure and one modern rooftop detail.

rows.text: Rooftop collection  ·  Groundwater recharge  ·  Check dams and ponds  ·  Types of degraded land

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Catch rain on a roof or behind a check dam, then store it or recharge groundwater.  ·  Filter out the first dirt. Do not send waste into the recharge pit.  ·  Benefits: a higher water table, dry-season supply, less flash flooding.  ·  Wasteland here means degraded land: erosion, salinity, mining spoil, waterlogging.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Water that is slowed on a slope infiltrates. Water that is sped up erodes.  ·  Salt accumulates at the surface when irrigation water evaporates and does not drain.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: How is a community pond a form of rainwater harvesting?

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: A saline field is not fixed by planting the same crop harder. It needs drainage or salt-tolerant species.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Rainwater harvesting is the deliberate collection of rain before it runs off into a drain and is lost. The water is stored in a tank or guided underground so a well or a spring can use it later. It is a way of keeping a local water supply, not a new source of river water from far away.  ·  A common design catches rain on a roof, sends it through a first-flush or a simple filter that drops leaves and grit, and then either fills a tank or leads the water into a recharge pit, a trench or an abandoned well. Check dams and percolation ponds do the same job for a slope: they slow the runoff so it soaks in instead of racing away.  ·  The gains are practical. The local water table rises, wells last longer into the dry months, and a sudden storm is less likely to flood the street because some of the water was held. In dry districts, traditional tanks and ponds did this long before the modern name. Rooftop collection has also been made compulsory in places such as Tamil Nadu.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Restoration by cover and drainage  ·  Repair with plants, contour bunds, drainage and a rest from grazing.  ·  First flush is the dirtier water at the start of a storm. Diverting it keeps the tank cleaner.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Contour bunds run across the slope, not down it. Downhill ditches speed erosion.  ·  Rainwater harvesting moves water into a tank or into the ground instead of into a storm drain.  ·  The repair of wasteland has to match the kind of damage.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Cover on a slope is what stops the next rain from cutting a new gully.  ·  Describe a rooftop system from the roof to the stored water.  ·  Give two kinds of wasteland and the matching repair.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Explain why a recharge pit must not receive sewage.  ·  Wasteland, in this chapter, is land so degraded that it no longer supports the use it once had. Gullied hills, salinity from bad irrigation, mining spoil, waterlogged soil and heavily overgrazed slopes are typical. It is not a wilderness that was always bare. It is land people damaged.  ·  The causes sit in how the land was used. Trees cut from a slope let rain tear the soil. Too many animals remove the cover. Irrigation water that cannot drain leaves salt at the surface. A mine leaves a pile that plants cannot root in. Each cause points at a repair, not at a single universal machine.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Development of that land means putting cover and water control back. Trees and grasses are planted. Contour bunds and check dams slow runoff. Waterlogged ground is drained. Salty ground is leached only where drainage exists, or it is given salt-tolerant plants. Grazing is held off until the cover returns.…  ·  # Rainwater harvesting and wasteland development ## 1.
